analysis.one_liner: Requires a fresh environmental review of oil and gas development before fracking proceeds on federal land in Central California.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past a House subcommittee; no vote was ever held.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would throw out a 2019 federal decision that opened the Bakersfield Field Office planning area to fracking and oil and gas leasing, and require a new, broader environmental review covering air quality, climate emissions, groundwater, water supplies, earthquakes, wildlife, and effects on low-income, minority, and Indigenous communities. The EPA would then review that study, and if it found serious impacts or insufficient information, the Bureau of Land Management would have to consult with the EPA before leasing federal land for oil and gas. The bill was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the Central California communities near federal oil and gas leases, including low-income residents, communities of color, and Tribes named in the bill, who would get a fuller accounting of pollution, groundwater, and health effects before drilling expands. The EPA also gains an explicit review role.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near Central California fracking sites

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies the December 2019 record of decision for the Bakersfield Field Office until the Bureau of Land Management completes a new supplemental environmental impact statement covering all oil and gas development in the planning area, not just fracking [S2][S3].

Requires the new study to examine air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, groundwater, surface water, seismicity, threatened and endangered species, and effects on low-income communities, communities of color, and Indigenous communities [S3].

Requires the EPA to review the new study within 180 days and requires the Bureau of Land Management to consult with the EPA before leasing if the EPA finds significant impacts or insufficient information [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies with leases or lease interests in the Bakersfield planning area, which would face a delay and possibly tighter conditions before drilling on federal land. Federal and state treasuries could see leasing revenue postponed during the new review.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies drilling federal land there

drawbacks.text: A new, broader environmental study would delay federal oil and gas leasing in the planning area, postponing energy production and the federal and state revenue that leasing generates [S2][S3].
The bill is narrow: it addresses one field office planning area, so its effect on statewide or national drilling, emissions, or consumer energy prices is small [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to nearby communities is a fuller, legally required look at air, water, and health effects before drilling expands; the cost is a delayed leasing process in one planning area. The tradeoff is modest in both directions because the bill covers a single planning area, but the review requirements are specific and the community-impact provisions go beyond standard practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on January 25, 2021, with Reps. Brownley and Panetta as cosponsors [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources on January 25, 2021, and to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on February 18, 2021 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators in the Bakersfield Field Office planning area are better off: the 2019 decision that opened the area to fracking and leasing was never displaced, so no new environmental review was required. Communities near the drilling did not get the broader study the bill would have mandated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators in that planning area

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring a new environmental impact statement for the Bakersfield Field Office planning area.

for.name: Reps. Julia Brownley and Jimmy Panetta

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on February 18, 2021, and never reported it out or scheduled a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all three sponsors and cosponsors were California House Democrats, so there is no record of where other members stood.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with federal leases in the Bakersfield Field Office planning area
industries.note: The bill would have nullified the 2019 decision opening the area to fracking and required a new environmental review and possible EPA consultation before leasing. Its main effect was to delay or constrain drilling on federal land in Central California, which is why it stalled in subcommittee.
